result.target_topic: Goodwill impairment testing methodology and Q4 2024 results

comparisons.peer_summary: The definition of a reporting unit and further details on goodwill and intangibles are provided in Note 7 of the Consolidated Financial Statements.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs provides detailed results of its 2024 goodwill impairment testing, whereas Bank of America's candidate D062 primarily serves as a cross-reference to Note 7 for definitions of reporting units and further details, without explicitly stating the 2024 impairment conclusion in the same sentence structure. Goldman Sachs explicitly states that 'In the fourth quarter of 2024, we performed our annual assessment... by performing a qualitative assessment' and found no impairment (gs_2024_7_P032_S010, gs_2024_7_P032_S011). Bank of America's text points readers to Note 7 for the 'definition of a reporting unit' and 'more information' regarding goodwill (bac_2024_7_P064_S007), lacking the specific 2024 outcome disclosure present in Goldman Sachs' primary text. Both relate to the governance and definition of reporting units in the context of goodwill, but Goldman Sachs provides the immediate test result while Bank of America directs to the notes.

sentences.text: In the fourth quarter of 2024, we performed our annual assessment of goodwill for impairment, for each of our reporting units with goodwill, by performing a qualitative assessment.
For more information, including the definition of a reporting unit, see Note 7 - Goodwill and Intangible Assets to the Consolidated Financial Statements.

comparisons.peer_summary: Decreases in fair value below carrying value for equity securities carried at cost or measurement alternative are recognized as income statement impairments, while other-than-temporary impairments for equity method investments are also recognized in earnings, requiring judgmental assessments.
comparisons.comparison: While Goldman Sachs focuses its Q4 2024 disclosure on goodwill impairment testing, Citi's peer candidate D495 addresses impairment recognition for equity securities carried at cost or under the measurement alternative. Both disclosures involve the concept of 'impairment' and the judgment required to assess value changes, but they apply to different asset classes (goodwill vs. equity securities). Citi notes that 'decreases in fair value below the carrying value are recognized as impairment in the Consolidated Statement of Income' for equity securities (c_2024_7_P672_S001) and that assessing if such decreases are 'other-than-temporary' is 'inherently judgmental' (c_2024_7_P672_S003). In contrast, Goldman Sachs' goodwill testing involved a qualitative determination that fair value exceeded carrying value, resulting in no impairment charge. The topics are related in their reliance on fair value assessments and management judgment, but distinct in the specific asset type and the fact that Goldman Sachs reported no impairment while Citi describes the conditions under which impairments are recognized.

sentences.text: In the fourth quarter of 2024, we performed our annual assessment of goodwill for impairment, for each of our reporting units with goodwill, by performing a qualitative assessment.
For equity securities carried at cost or under the measurement alternative, decreases in fair value below the carrying value are recognized as impairment in the Consolidated Statement of Income.
Assessing if the fair value impairment is temporary is also inherently judgmental.

comparisons.peer_topic: 2024 Goodwill impairment conclusion and fair value headroom
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm concluded that goodwill was not impaired as of December 31, 2024, noting that for each reporting unit, fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10%.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase conducted annual goodwill impairment tests in Q4 2024 and concluded that no impairment was required because the fair value of each reporting unit exceeded its carrying value. Goldman Sachs determined this via qualitative assessment, stating it was 'more likely than not that the estimated fair value... exceeded its respective carrying value' (gs_2024_7_P032_S010, gs_2024_7_P032_S011). JPMorgan similarly concluded 'goodwill was not impaired as of December 31, 2024,' noting that for each reporting unit, 'fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10%' (jpm_2024_7_P799_S002, jpm_2024_7_P799_S003). While both found fair value to be above carrying value, JPMorgan quantifies the headroom (at least 10%) whereas Goldman Sachs relies on the qualitative 'more likely than not' threshold without specifying the magnitude of the excess in this specific sentence.

sentences.text: In the fourth quarter of 2024, we performed our annual assessment of goodwill for impairment, for each of our reporting units with goodwill, by performing a qualitative assessment.
As a result of the annual assessment, we determined that it was more likely than not that the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with goodwill exceeded its respective carrying value.
Based on such reviews, the Firm has concluded that goodwill was not impaired as of December 31, 2024.

For each of the reporting units, fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10% and there was no indication of a significant risk of goodwill impairment based on current projections and valuations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Result of annual goodwill impairment testing
comparisons.peer_summary: At each annual goodwill impairment testing date, each reporting unit with goodwill had a fair value substantially in excess of its carrying value.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both reported that their goodwill impairment tests for 2024 resulted in fair values substantially exceeding carrying values for all reporting units with goodwill, indicating no impairment. Goldman Sachs' qualitative assessment concluded that 'the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with goodwill exceeded its respective carrying value' (gs_2024_7_P032_S011). Similarly, Morgan Stanley stated that 'each of our reporting units with goodwill had a fair value that was substantially in excess of its carrying value' (ms_2024_7_P125_S001). Both disclosures reflect a similar outcome of robust fair value headroom, though Morgan Stanley uses the descriptive term 'substantially in excess' while Goldman Sachs confirms the exceedance based on the 'more likely than not' qualitative threshold.
